Levant update: The softer-than-expected BRC print will provide modest comfort to Bank of England rate-setters looking for evidence that consumer price pressures are easing, though the data covers a narrower basket than the official CPI measure and is unlikely to move the needle materially on rate expectations alone.

The divergence between firm-level trading optimism and weaker economy-wide confidence in the Lloyds survey suggests businesses are managing their own books reasonably well even as the macro backdrop deteriorates, a nuance that complicates the BoE's read on demand conditions.

Manufacturing's 10-point confidence collapse to its lowest relative to its 12-month average is the sharpest warning signal in the data and points to ongoing vulnerability in the goods-producing sector.

Sterling may find limited support from the benign inflation print but the Lloyds data is unlikely to generate sustained upside momentum. --- UK shop price inflation held at 1.2% in June, below forecasts, as food costs eased and summer promotions cushioned non-food prices, while a Lloyds survey showed business confidence falling for a third consecutive month.

The BRC's monthly survey of major retail chains, based on data collected in the first week of June, showed food price inflation easing to 2.4%, its lowest reading since March 2025, down from 2.7% in May.

Fresh food prices rose 2.8% on the year, a meaningful deceleration from the 3.4% recorded the previous month, driven in part by an unusually abundant strawberry harvest and retailer promotions on ice cream and chilled products as Britain experienced a spell of hot weather.

Non-food prices edged higher, rising 0.6% annually compared with 0.5% in May, as discounting on clothing and footwear ahead of the summer season was insufficient to pull the overall reading lower.

Goods-flow update: The launch of a formal EU-China trade consultation mechanism reduces the near-term risk of an escalatory tariff exchange between Brussels and Beijing, offering some relief to European industries most exposed to Chinese import competition.

Rare earth and critical mineral supply chains are the most immediate beneficiary, with China's assurances over existing export controls providing a degree of certainty for European manufacturers dependent on those inputs.

The October timeline creates a defined catalyst for markets to assess progress, with the EU leaders summit on October 15 adding political weight to the deadline.

A failure to deliver tangible results by then would likely reignite deficit-driven trade friction and could accelerate EU consideration of defensive measures against subsidised Chinese goods. --- The EU and China launched a new trade consultation mechanism in Brussels on Monday, setting an October deadline for tangible progress on a €360 billion annual trade deficit, export controls, and rare earth supply chain stability.

Summary: The EU and China held inaugural Trade and Investment Consultations in Brussels on June 29, with the first China-EU joint trade statement since 2019 issued following the meeting The mechanism covers four streams: trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights, and WTO reform; a working group on trade balance launches immediately with a joint monitoring mechanism to track trade flows The EU's trade deficit with China reached €360 billion last year, equivalent to roughly €1 billion per day, affecting all 27 member states Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said he will visit China in October and expects to present first tangible results by then, with a progress assessment due in September and a roadmap with deliverables to follow in coming days China provided assurances that existing export controls on rare earths and permanent magnets will not disrupt EU supply chains; Beijing had briefly curbed rare earth exports during a tariff dispute with the United States last autumn German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche met Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao over the weekend and called for closer cooperation on the basis of open markets and a level playing field The European Union and China launched a formal trade consultation mechanism in Brussels on Monday, setting an October deadline for measurable progress on a commercial relationship strained by a €360 billion annual trade deficit, disputed export controls and European dependence on Chinese critical materials.

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao authorised officials to begin structured work across four areas: rebalancing trade and investment flows, managing export controls on rare earths and other critical raw materials, protecting intellectual property rights, and advancing World Trade Organization reform.

The two sides also issued a joint statement, the first of its kind since 2019, signalling a political commitment to managing tensions through dialogue rather than escalation. Šefčovič said he would travel to China in October, at which point he expected to present the first concrete results of the process.

A preliminary assessment of progress is due in September, with a roadmap of expected deliverables to be published within days.
